p01.reason: With 'no longer' it denies rule A's per-request gateway lookup of the sessions table, and new.md never tells its reader that such a lookup existed; the sessions table appears nowhere else in it.

p02.reason: It sets the present fixed expiry against rule A's sliding expiry, where every accepted request pushed the expiry forward by 30 days, and new.md never presents that sliding expiry.

p03.reason: With 'no longer' it denies rule A's per-request lookup of the auth service's token store before a request was served, and new.md never says such a lookup existed.

p04.reason: It sets reading the expiry from the claims against a countdown timer in the app, an alternative that neither old.md (where the app never renews) nor new.md presents.

p05.reason: It sets scheduled key rotation against rotation in response to an incident, which neither document presents; old.md has no signing keys at all.

p06.licence: Many mobile apps keep tokens in shared preferences on Android or in user defaults on iOS.
p06.reason: It contrasts Lumen's storage with the plain stores that new.md introduced in the sentence just before it.

p07.licence: The OAuth specification also allows a refresh token to stay the same for its whole life.
p07.reason: It declines the option that new.md presented in the sentence just before it, and the refresh token does not exist in rule A.

p08.licence: The payments service keeps its own stricter rule that a card operation needs an access token issued less than five minutes ago.
p08.reason: It contrasts every other service with the payments service's stricter rule, which new.md states in the sentence just before it.

p09.reason: It is a guarantee about what an access token never carries, and it sets the token against no other design and touches nothing of rule A, whose opaque token carried no claims.

p10.reason: It gives the default behaviour when the refresh endpoint is unreachable, without setting it against any other design and without touching rule A's 401 handling.
